catalog_quote: In most words all syllables are accentuated alike, a very slight stress being perhaps laid on the penultimate. This is more particularly noticeable when the last syllable but one contains a long vowel, e. g. ol-ayóni, 'n-joníto. Should the accent fall on any other syllable but the penultimate, it is specially marked, thus: ol-móruo, kewárie. ... [p. 8] The accent, such as it is, does not fall on the penultimate in the following cases: I. When the subject of a verb is the first person plural, the last syllable is always slightly accentuated. Examples: Ki-súj, we follow (him). Ki-tu-suj-á, we have followed (him). ... II. Whenever one of two a's falls out before i in verbs commencing with the latter letter, the remaining a is rather more strongly sounded than the other syllables: Á-isuj-a (for aa-isuj-a), I washed thee, or he or they washed me. ... The difference is marked by raising or lowering the voice at the end of the substantive, and the following rule is invariable. If the subject is the substantive, the voice is raised as in asking a question; if the subject is the pronoun, the voice is lowered as when finishing a sentence
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is weak and nearly level across syllables; where perceptible it tends to the penultimate syllable, most clearly when the penult vowel is long. Words with non-penultimate accent are marked individually in the book (ol-móruo, kewárie). The same pages then describe raising/lowering of the voice at word end as the invariable marker of subject vs object (an early observation of Maa grammatical tone), so the book treats pitch, not stress, as the contrastive prosody.
new_statements.exceptions: (I) verbs with 1st-person-plural subject take slight final-syllable stress (ki-súj, ki-tu-suj-á); (II) when aa- contracts to a- before i-initial verb stems the surviving a is more strongly sounded (á-isuj-a); lexical items marked with non-penultimate accent (ol-móruo, kewárie). Note that Hinde 1901 (p. 2, also saved) gives a conflicting impressionistic rule: accent usually on the first syllable of disyllables, otherwise mostly the second syllable, 'not very regular', some words with all syllables equal.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms of nouns and inflected verbs; the p. 8 voice raising/lowering rule concerns word-final pitch in the sentence (subject vs object marking).
new_statements.identity_note: the Harvard library catalogue 1905 and Hinde 1901 describe the Maasai of British East Africa (Kenya; the Harvard library catalogue distinguishes 'Northern' and 'Southern' Masai forms), i.e. language-level masa1300. Karani 2018 (silent on stress) describes the Parakuyo dialect of Tanzania; Levergood 1987 (not opened) describes Arusa (Arusha), also a Maa dialect. Modern sources (Payne; WALS 13A) treat Maa as a two-tone (H/L) language.

new_statements.quote: This data shows that the behavior of pitch active in Maa today is more “free” than we would expect from a system based on accent, allowing separate contrast on essentially each mora, indicating a tone system. [p. 17] … Without any phonetic studies of Il-Keekonyokie Maa pitch and stress/accent, or even anecdotal evidence relating length, volume, etc. and pitch, I must remain silent regarding the complexity of the phonetic realization of stress. [p. 18] … For each criterion which indicates one or the other type of system, then, the system active in Il-Keekonyokie Maa fits Hyman’s description of a tonal system. [p. 19]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: native text, title page 'A THESIS.. Master of Arts, March 2002'). Verified by extracted text on single pages: 'This data shows that the behavior of pitch active in Maa today is more "free" than we would expect from a system based on accent, allowing separate contrast on essentially each mora, indicating a tone system' is on printed p. 17 = p. 32; 'Without any phonetic studies of Il-Keekonyokie Maa pitch and stress/accent, or even anecdotal evidence relating length, volume, etc. and pitch, I must remain silent regarding the complexity of the phonetic realization of stress' on p. 18 = PDF 33; 'For each criterion which indicates one or the other type of system, then, the system active in Il-Ke…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tone language with a stress statement' reading from the Harvard library catalogue 1905. Rasmussen gives the explicit typological argument that Maa is a tone (not accent) language, states that stress is unstudied phonetically (so he neither confirms nor denies the Harvard library catalogue's 'very slight stress.. perhaps on the penultimate'), and adds the observation that H tone is confined to a final three-mora window. No placement claim, so no contradiction. Dialect: Il-Keekonyokie (Kenyan Maasai section).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Il-Keekonyokie Maa is a tone language by every one of Hyman's tone-vs-stress criteria for which there is data (14 distinct tone patterns over 3 morae, far more than the n+1 an accent system allows; more than one H or L locus per word; distinctive rather than demarcative function; tone rules of the assimilatory kind). The author explicitly declines to say anything about stress placement or its phonetic realization for lack of phonetic study, and finds no evidence of syllable weight affecting pitch. On p. 85 he adds that a High tone reliably falls on the ultimate, penultimate or antepenultimate mora, 'suspiciously close to some kind of stress system', but treats this as a question for Proto-Maa reconstruction, not a synchronic stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: 'except in a few cases' the H tone falls outside the last three morae (p. 85); non-automatic downstep phrase-finally in declaratives is the one demarcative-like effect noted (pp. 18-19).
new_statements.identity_note: Rasmussen 2002 describes Il-Keekonyokie Maa, a Kenyan Maasai section (Rift Valley); it is an MA thesis, not a PhD, and the PDF has 262 pages. Reinisch 1874 describes Barea (Nara, nara1262, Eritrea), not Maa at all; its attachment to masa1300 is a misattribution in the source list. the Harvard library catalogue 1905 (existing statement) is Kenyan Maasai generally.

sources.citation: Hinde, Hildegarde (1901). The Masai Language: Grammatical Notes together with a Vocabulary. Cambridge: University Press.
sources.note: p. 2 (verified on page scan): 'The accent in Masai usually falls on the first syllable in words of two syllables, and in words of two or three syllables most usually on the second, but occasionally on the third. In words of more than three syllables the accent is usually on the second syllable. The accentuation is, however, not very regular, and in some words all the syllables are of equal value.' Preface p. v: the name Masai itself has 'the accent very markedly on the first syllable'. Non-linguist author; impressionistic.

sources.note: In a number of East African Nilotic languages case is marked exclusively by tonal differentiation; this is 'fully described in Maasai (Tucker and Mpaayei, 1955)' and all investigated Kalenjin dialects, present in Teso, apparently lacking in Luo; the paper analyses the tonal nominative/absolutive marking comparatively.
sources.venue: Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies
